questions.question: What is the worst-case lookup cost of a linear scan over n items?
options: O(n), because an unsuccessful search may inspect every item
O(log n), because every comparison discards half the input
Expected O(1), because the target maps directly to a bucket
O(n log n), because the input must be sorted before each comparison

questions.question: Which precondition does binary search require?
options: A linked structure whose nodes are allocated in random locations
A sorted collection that supports efficient random access by position
A hash function with a load factor strictly equal to one
An unsorted stream that can be consumed only from beginning to end

questions.topic: Time Complexity of Linear Scan vs Binary Search vs Hash Probe
questions.question: About how many worst-case comparisons does binary search need for one million sorted IDs?
options: About ten, because ten squared is close to one million
About one thousand, because it searches the square root of the input
About twenty, because 2 raised to 20 slightly exceeds one million
About one million, because every unsuccessful lookup scans the entire array

questions.topic: Time Complexity of Linear Scan vs Binary Search vs Hash Probe
questions.question: Why is describing every hash lookup as guaranteed O(1) inaccurate?
options: A hash table must sort all keys before it can calculate a bucket
A hash probe always examines every allocated bucket in key order
Hashing requires a balanced tree whose height is logarithmic
Severe collisions can make a bucket contain n entries and require linear work

questions.topic: Time Complexity of Linear Scan vs Binary Search vs Hash Probe
questions.question: There is one query against an unsorted dataset, after which the dataset will be discarded. Which strategy is usually most defensible?
options: Scan once rather than pay O(n log n) to sort for one logarithmic lookup
Sort first because O(n log n) construction is always less work than O(n) scanning
Build both a tree and hash table because preprocessing cost never affects the choice
Use binary search directly because sorted order is optional for a single query

questions.topic: Time Complexity of Linear Scan vs Binary Search vs Hash Probe
questions.question: Why can a linear scan beat binary search on a small contiguous array?
options: A scan has a better asymptotic bound than logarithmic search for every n
Sequential reads can avoid branch and cache-miss costs that dominate tiny inputs
A scan constructs a constant-time hash index while comparing the first element
Sequential reads allow the scan to omit equality comparisons entirely

questions.topic: Big-O of Intersecting Two Sorted Lists
questions.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of two-cursor intersection for sorted lists of lengths m and n?
options: O(mn), because every value from one list is compared with every value from the other
O(log m + log n), because both cursors discard half a list per comparison
O(m + n), because neither cursor advances more than its own list length
Expected O(1), because document IDs are automatically placed in hash buckets

questions.topic: Big-O of Intersecting Two Sorted Lists
questions.question: When two cursor values match during sorted-list intersection, what happens?
options: Emit the smaller value and reset both cursors to the list beginnings
Discard the matching value and advance only the cursor in the longer list
Binary-search both complete lists again before accepting the candidate
Emit the value and advance both cursors because that occurrence is resolved

questions.question: One postings list has 10 entries and another has 10 million. Which method can avoid scanning most of the long list?
options: Merge both lists fully because O(m+n) is always physically smallest
Iterate the short list and binary-search each value in the long list
Sort the short list once for every value encountered in the long list
Materialize the Cartesian product and filter its 100 million pairs

questions.topic: Big-O of Intersecting Two Sorted Lists
questions.question: Why should an AND query generally process the rarest term first?
options: Rare terms have the longest lists and therefore maximize intermediate candidates
Rare terms make sorted order unnecessary for every later operation
The first intersection can produce at most the size of its smallest input
The rarest term guarantees that every candidate satisfies all remaining terms

Skipping requires rebuilding both lists as unsorted linked structures
Skipping can operate only when the two input lengths are relatively prime
Producing ten million required results alone takes at least proportional work

questions.topic: Memory Hierarchy: Why Sequential Access Beats Random Access
questions.question: What is spatial locality?
options: Accessing nearby addresses so one fetched block supplies several useful values
Accessing unrelated addresses so every value requires a separate memory request
Keeping every dataset permanently inside CPU registers regardless of its size
Hashing each key into a different storage service before comparing its value

questions.topic: Memory Hierarchy: Why Sequential Access Beats Random Access
questions.question: Why do random pointer-chasing accesses often stall a processor?
options: They always transfer fewer bytes than a single register can contain
The next address is unknown until the current node arrives, limiting prefetch
They make every cache line contain the entire remaining linked structure
The processor converts each pointer chain into one vectorized sequential instruction

questions.topic: Memory Hierarchy: Why Sequential Access Beats Random Access
questions.question: A 400 MB array is scanned at 20 GB/s effective bandwidth. What is the byte-transfer floor before comparison overhead?
options: About 20 seconds
About 2 seconds
About 0.02 seconds
About 0.00002 seconds

questions.topic: Memory Hierarchy: Why Sequential Access Beats Random Access
questions.question: Why is two-cursor postings intersection especially friendly to modern hardware?
options: It performs unpredictable jumps between unrelated heap objects for every comparison
It hashes every posting into a remote bucket before advancing either cursor
It repeatedly reloads earlier postings so the cache cannot reuse a line
It walks compact arrays forward, enabling cache-line reuse and prefetching

questions.topic: Memory Hierarchy: Why Sequential Access Beats Random Access
questions.question: How can compression make postings traversal faster despite adding decode arithmetic?
options: It can reduce transferred cache lines and storage pages enough to outweigh decoding
It converts sequential arrays into scattered nodes that require more memory misses
It increases postings bytes so the CPU has more independent work to pipeline
It removes sorted order and therefore eliminates all cursor comparisons

questions.topic: Memory Hierarchy: Why Sequential Access Beats Random Access
questions.question: When should a cached hash probe still beat a sequential scan?
options: When finding one key would otherwise require reading hundreds of megabytes
When the hash table requires one remote read for every item in the corpus
When every query needs to evaluate an unindexed predicate over all records
When the scan's complete working set already fits inside one CPU register
